summary: Describes the Optimized Link State Routing (OLSR) protocol for mobile ad hoc networks. It tailors classical link-state routing to wireless networks by using multipoint relays, selected nodes that forward broadcast messages, to reduce flooding overhead. The RFC is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: OLSR lets nodes in a mobile ad hoc network maintain routes by exchanging information regularly. Selected neighbors relay broadcasts, which reduces the number of retransmissions compared with having every node repeat every message.

subtitle: A proactive routing protocol that uses selected relays to reduce flooding in mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: In a mobile ad hoc network, having every node retransmit every control message creates unnecessary radio traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Each node selects symmetric neighbors as multipoint relays; those relays retransmit broadcasts and provide the link information used to calculate routes.
tldr.outcome: OLSR reduces control-message retransmissions and calculates routes by hop count. RFC 3626 is Experimental and specifies no special security measures.

today: RFC 3626 is an Experimental RFC published in October 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Proactive Routing Protocol
sections.content:
OLSR is a table-driven protocol for mobile ad hoc networks. Nodes exchange topology information regularly, so routes are available when data needs to be sent. The protocol is distributed and does not depend on a central controller.

OLSR uses partial link-state information to calculate routes with the lowest number of hops. The RFC says the method is particularly suited to large, dense networks and traffic between many changing pairs of nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: OLSR keeps route information ready before a node needs to send data. Each node builds its own routing view from information shared by nearby nodes.

sections.title: Selecting Multipoint Relays
sections.content:
Each node selects a set of symmetric one-hop neighbors as multipoint relays (MPRs). The set must reach every symmetric strict two-hop neighbor. A neighbor that is not selected still receives and processes broadcasts, but does not retransmit broadcasts from that node.

Nodes learn which neighbors selected them through periodic HELLO messages. A node also advertises its willingness to forward traffic, using a value from 0 to 7; a value of 0 means it must not be selected, while 7 means it must be selected.
sections.plainLanguage: A node selects nearby relays that together can reach the nodes two steps away. Only selected relays repeat its broadcasts, and each node can indicate how willing it is to forward traffic.

sections.title: Messages and Topology Information
sections.content:
OLSR packets use UDP on port 698 and contain one or more messages. A common message header carries the originator address, a validity time, a time-to-live, a hop count, and a sequence number. Nodes track duplicates so they do not process or retransmit the same message repeatedly.

HELLO messages stay within the neighborhood and support link sensing, neighbor detection, and MPR signaling. Topology Control messages are flooded by MPRs to advertise links to MPR selectors. MID messages associate multiple interface addresses with one node’s main address, and HNA messages describe external networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each OLSR message says who created it and how long it remains useful. HELLO messages describe nearby links, while topology messages help all nodes build routes.

sections.title: Calculating Routes and Security
sections.content:
Each node calculates a routing table from its symmetric neighbors, two-hop neighbors, and topology information learned from TC messages. Entries identify a destination and the next hop used to reach it. The RFC proposes regular HELLO and TC refresh intervals and recommends random jitter to reduce synchronized transmissions.

The RFC does not specify special security measures. It warns that control messages reveal topology on an unprotected wireless network and that nodes can advertise false information or replay old messages. It recommends message authentication where needed and says information should be checked before it is injected into another routing domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node combines neighborhood and topology information to choose routes with the fewest hops. Because OLSR does not secure these messages itself, deployments may need encryption and authentication.
